title: Self-Driving Laboratories for Formulation: Handling Liquids, Pastes, Powders and Objects, from Robots to Digital Twins and AI Agents

affiliations.a: Acceleration Consortium, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3H6, Canada
affiliations.b: SEKISUI Chemical Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan

abstract: Formulation, combining liquids, pastes and powders into products whose properties emerge from both composition and process, is a promising but comparatively under-automated target for self-driving laboratories (SDLs). An autonomous formulation experiment is a physical choreography: ingredients of very different rheology are dosed into one premix container, which is carried to a mixer, processed and characterized, often with materials the robot has never handled. Landmark SDLs show that this physical layer, the handling of materials and the manipulation of the containers that hold them, can limit autonomy as much as the planning algorithm. Yet reviews of the field have mostly treated it as a platform detail. This review examines the methods, trends and open challenges of automating formulation, following a representative workflow through an SDL. We examine how viscosity, yield stress and powder flowability affect dispensing and review how recent studies use sensing, modeling and feedback to handle liquids, semi-solids and powders; compare gantry, SCARA, articulated, collaborative and mobile robots for moving premix containers and tools; and compare commercial dispensers and integrated platforms, finding that price tracks mechanism and ecosystem rather than accuracy and is rarely public, so that researchers can match dispensing methods, robots and platforms to their formulation tasks. We then show how low-cost retrofits extend platforms beyond their factory specifications, how simulation and digital twins let a laboratory rehearse and verify a workflow before material is committed, how system architecture and orchestration software integrate the devices into one laboratory, and how data, machine learning and AI agents, connected through APIs and data pipelines, choose the next experiment. We close with shared benchmarks (reference materials and handling tasks), open interfaces, calibrated twins and safeguards that a laboratory able to formulate with any ingredient will need.

figure_captions.1: A formulation SDL and its digital twin. Physical cell (left): a CNC gantry with dispenser rack and balance (1–3), a SCARA elevator serving two characterizers (4–6) and an arm loading the mixer (7, 8). Digital twin (right): robot trajectories (A), material models (B), virtual sensors (C) and GPU simulation (D) rehearse each step before it runs.
figure_captions.2: Material properties and handling mechanisms: (A) liquids to pastes and (B) powders by cohesion; (C, E, G) selection charts and (D, F, H) mechanisms for liquids, semi-solids and powders. Product photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Hamilton [16], Nordson EFD [17] and XQ Instruments; powder dispensers are compared in [18].
figure_captions.3: Literature scenarios titled by their sense–act sequence and adapted from the cited studies: liquids (A–H) [11,22,23,24,25,26,27,28], semi-solids (I–L) [31,32,33,34] and powders and granular media (M–T) [12,37,38,39,40,41,42,43].
figure_captions.4: Robot classes for object handling, ordered by axes, reach and cost: (A) Cartesian gantry, (B) SCARA, (C) 6-DOF arm, (D) 7-DOF or dual-arm cobot and (E) mobile manipulator; (F) repeatability versus price (Table 2).
figure_captions.5: (A) Commercial dispensers and platforms by material class, mechanism and price (hollow markers: quote only; bracketed numbers: references). (B–E) Qualitative 0–10 profiles of four platforms (‘solid handling’: labware transfer). Photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Chemspeed [71], Hamilton [16] and Eppendorf [75].
figure_captions.6: Four fidelity levels of a formulation twin, (A) workflow, (B) kinematics, (C) contact dynamics and (D) material physics, at rising compute cost, with example tools (SimPy, MoveIt 2, MuJoCo, Isaac Lab; screenshots and logos from the projects’ repositories under MIT, BSD-3-Clause and Apache-2.0 licenses; logos are trademarks of their owners).
figure_captions.7: The digital twin as a working environment: (A) motion planning in ROS 2 with MoveIt 2, (B) a GPU simulator interface, (C) a DEM/MPM material solver and (D) rehearsal of AI-proposed plans before release to the cell.
figure_captions.8: Architecture of a formulation SDL: (A) execution and equipment hierarchies, (B) functional layers of orchestration software and (C) functions provided by eight open-source systems (details in Supplementary Table S1).
figure_captions.9: The decision ladder: data (bottom), models that choose the next experiment (middle) and AI agents (top), connected to the robots by software and data pipelines (right).
